# Token-Bucket Admission Control

This example protects a catalogue API from excessive requests. The request is
the trust boundary: an attacker can send more work than the application and
database can safely serve. The vulnerable baseline keys an in-memory bucket by
the source IP address. That is not a reliable client identity, its state is
unbounded, and every application instance makes an independent decision.

The safer fixture authenticates workshop clients and applies a bounded,
per-client token budget with different costs for simple and bulk reads. It
returns `429 Too Many Requests` when a request cannot be admitted. The local
fixture is deliberately single-instance; a production policy needs equivalent
enforcement at a trusted gateway or in shared, bounded rate-limit storage.

The catalogue deliberately uses numeric database IDs only. Predictable public
identifiers can enable enumeration and data disclosure, but that is outside this
admission-control exercise; see [URL Data Leak](../url-data-leak/) for that
separate concern.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- identify request volume as an availability and resource-management threat;
- explain why a remote IP address is not a trustworthy client quota identity;
- demonstrate a failing admission-control regression test against the baseline;
- verify a bounded, authenticated-client policy that returns `429`; and
- state why a single-JVM limiter does not enforce a production-wide policy.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25 or newer](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- `rsync` available on your PATH to install and clean up workshop fixtures.

- `curl` available on your PATH to exercise the local HTTP API.

## The program to inspect

The baseline uses `HttpServletRequest.getRemoteAddr()` as its client key and
keeps buckets in a controller-local `HashMap`. Reverse proxies and NAT can make
unrelated clients share a key; distributed clients can evade a per-IP quota; and
each JVM starts with an empty map. This is an intentional insecure design
baseline, not a production recommendation.

```java
public final class CatalogueItemController {

    private static final Logger LOGGER = LoggerFactory.getLogger(CatalogueItemController.class);

    private final CatalogueItemService service;
    private final Bandwidth limit;
    private final Map<String, Bucket> ipToBucket = new HashMap<>();

    public CatalogueItemController(final CatalogueItemService service) {
        this.service = requireNonNull(service, "Service cannot be null");

        // Configure the rate limit
        limit = Bandwidth.builder()
                .capacity(20)
                .refillGreedy(20, Duration.ofMinutes(1))
                .build();
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<CatalogueItemTo> get(
            @PathVariable(value = "id") final long id,
            final HttpServletRequest request) {
        // Here's where the basic rate limit happens
        final Bucket bucket = getBucket(request.getRemoteAddr());
        if (!bucket.tryConsume(1)) {
            return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.TOO_MANY_REQUESTS).build();
        }

        return service.findById(id)
                .map(CatalogueItemTo::of)
                .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
                .orElseGet(() -> ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }

    @GetMapping("/all/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<List<CatalogueItemTo>> getAll(
            @PathVariable(value = "id") final Set<Long> ids,
            final HttpServletRequest request) {
        final Bucket bucket = getBucket(request.getRemoteAddr());
        if (!bucket.tryConsume(1)) {
            return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.TOO_MANY_REQUESTS).build();
        }

        return ResponseEntity.ok(
                service.findAllById(ids).stream()
                        .map(CatalogueItemTo::of)
                        .collect(Collectors.toList()));
    }

    private Bucket getBucket(final String remoteAddress) {
        LOGGER.info("retrieving token bucket for user at {}", remoteAddress);

        Bucket result = ipToBucket.get(remoteAddress);
        if (result == null) {
            result = Bucket.builder()
                    .addLimit(limit)
                    .build();
            ipToBucket.put(remoteAddress, result);
        }
        return result;
    }
}
```

The fixture makes the identity boundary explicit through authenticated workshop
users, charges bulk reads more than simple reads, and rejects new identities
once its local tracking limit is full. The constants are teaching values; real
limits require capacity modelling and operational review.

```java
public final class ClientRateLimiter {

    private static final int MAX_TRACKED_CLIENTS = 1_000;
    private static final long CAPACITY = 20;

    private static final Bandwidth LIMIT = Bandwidth.builder()
            .capacity(CAPACITY)
            .refillGreedy(CAPACITY, Duration.ofMinutes(1))
            .build();

    private final Map<String, Bucket> buckets = new HashMap<>();

    public boolean tryConsume(final String clientId, final long cost) {
        if (cost <= 0 || cost > CAPACITY) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Cost must be between 1 and " + CAPACITY);
        }

        return bucketFor(clientId)
                .tryConsume(cost);
    }

    private synchronized Bucket bucketFor(final String clientId) {
        Bucket bucket = buckets.get(clientId);
        if (bucket == null) {
            if (buckets.size() >= MAX_TRACKED_CLIENTS) {
                return null;
            }
            bucket = Bucket.builder().addLimit(LIMIT).build();
            buckets.put(clientId, bucket);
        }

        return bucket;
    }
}
```

## Guided walkthrough

Run these commands from this example directory. Fixture-copy steps alter the
local source tree temporarily; their cleanup restores the intentional baseline.

1. Build the baseline.

   Its tests demonstrate the insecure contract: requests are anonymous, and
   every caller behind the same source address shares one quota. Passing tests
   confirm that the vulnerable baseline behaves as shown; they do not approve
   the policy for deployment.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the application was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 1 --prune './target'
   ```

   The packaged Spring Boot JAR and the original thin JAR.

   ```
   ./target
   ├── token-bucket-1.0.0.jar
   └── token-bucket-1.0.0.jar.original

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

2. Start the vulnerable baseline locally.

   The PID file identifies only this workshop process and lets the runbook stop
   it during cleanup.

   ```shell
   java -jar 'target/token-bucket-1.0.0.jar' > 'target/application.log' 2>&1 &
   echo $! > 'target/application.pid'

   # Wait for the application to start
   until curl --silent --fail http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item/1 >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
   ```

3. The startup check was the first anonymous request.

   Send 19 additional anonymous requests from the same local source address.
   Each returns `200`.

   ```shell
   for attempt in {1..19}; do
     curl --silent --fail --output /dev/null \
       'http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item/1'
   done
   ```

   Send the 21st anonymous request. It returns `429 Too Many Requests`.

   ```shell
   curl \
     --silent \
     --fail \
     --output /dev/null \
     --write-out '%{http_code}\n' \
     'http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item/1'
   ```

   The final anonymous request receives `429`; curl fails because `--fail`
   converts that HTTP error response into exit code `22`.

   ```
   429
   ```

   Two distinct clients behind the same NAT or reverse proxy would share this quota, while a caller that can arrive from
   another address gets a different bucket. Inspect the regression tests that
   specify the remediation.

   They require an authenticated client, independent quotas for Alice and Bob, a
   higher cost for bulk reads, and `429` after the bucket is exhausted.

4. Reproduce the problem as a test.

   The `fixtures` directory contains an updated version of the test that reproduces the issue.

   ```java
   class CatalogueItemControllerTest {

       @Autowired
       private MockMvc mockMvc;

       @Test
       void requiresAnAuthenticatedClient() throws Exception {
           mockMvc.perform(get("/catalogue/item/1"))
                   .andExpect(status().isUnauthorized());
       }

       @Test
       void limitsEachAuthenticatedClientIndependently() throws Exception {
           for (int attempt = 0; attempt < 20; attempt++) {
               mockMvc.perform(get("/catalogue/item/1").with(httpBasic("alice", "alice-password")))
                       .andExpect(status().isOk());
           }

           mockMvc.perform(get("/catalogue/item/1").with(httpBasic("alice", "alice-password")))
                   .andExpect(status().isTooManyRequests());
           mockMvc.perform(get("/catalogue/item/1").with(httpBasic("bob", "bob-password")))
                   .andExpect(status().isOk());
       }

       @Test
       void chargesBulkReadsMoreThanSimpleReads() throws Exception {
           mockMvc.perform(get("/catalogue/item/all/1").with(httpBasic("alice", "alice-password")))
                   .andExpect(status().isOk());

           for (int attempt = 0; attempt < 15; attempt++) {
               mockMvc.perform(get("/catalogue/item/1").with(httpBasic("alice", "alice-password")))
                       .andExpect(status().isOk());
           }
           mockMvc.perform(get("/catalogue/item/1").with(httpBasic("alice", "alice-password")))
                   .andExpect(status().isTooManyRequests());
       }
   }
   ```

   Copy the fixture tests only and build. The build should fail because the
   baseline has neither Spring Security nor the secure controller contract.

   ```shell
   cp 'fixtures/pom.xml' 'pom.xml'
   rsync --archive 'fixtures/src/test' 'src'
   ```

   Run the fixture tests. They should fail because the vulnerable baseline has
   no authenticated-client policy, independent client quotas, or endpoint-cost
   rules required by the safer admission-control contract.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   The fixture tests fail because the vulnerable baseline does not yet implement
   the authenticated, per-client admission-control contract.

   ```
   ...
   [ERROR] Failures:
   [ERROR]   CatalogueItemControllerTest.chargesBulkReadsMoreThanSimpleReads:44 Status expected:<200> but was:<401>
   [ERROR]   CatalogueItemControllerTest.limitsEachAuthenticatedClientIndependently:32 Status expected:<200> but was:<401>
   [INFO]
   [ERROR] Tests run: 3, Failures: 2, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
   [INFO]
   [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
   [INFO] BUILD FAILURE
   [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
   ...
   ```

5. Address the issue.

   The fixture retains Bucket4j while adding Spring Security and security-test
   support; its source remains under the `demo` package and the application
   entry point remains `demo.Main`.

   ```shell
   rsync --archive 'fixtures/src/main' 'src'
   ```

   The fixture's workshop-only Basic Auth users are `alice` / `alice-password`
   and `bob` / `bob-password`. It is useful for demonstrating a trusted client
   identity, but static in-memory users and a local in-process map are not a
   deployment design.

   Build the project again. The regression test should now pass.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   All tests pass, including the regression test.

   ```
   ...
   [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
   [INFO] BUILD SUCCESS
   [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
   ...
   ```

   The tests now pass. They verify the admission policy without sleeping for a
   real refill period; Bucket4j owns the token accounting and refill timing.

6. Stop the local server.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat target/application.pid)" 2>/dev/null || true
   ```

## Key takeaways and residual risk

- A rate limit is a security requirement for resource management, not a library
  dependency.
- Remote addresses do not reliably identify a client or establish a fair quota.
- Authentication, bounded state, endpoint cost, and fail-closed `429` responses
  make the local policy clearer and testable.
- Production systems still need trustworthy identity propagation, shared
  enforcement across instances, monitoring, and limits based on measured
  resource cost.
